bp: Misinformation on social media is not only a pile of false posts waiting to be labeled. It is also a stream of human reactions: people read, click, comment, share, ignore, or return later, and those actions help decide how far a claim travels. This paper serves the problem of predicting that reaction stream across platforms. The practical need is clear: a misleading post that receives little response is different from one that keeps drawing attention, emotion, and reward from users over time. The paper treats engagement as a social exchange. In ordinary terms, a user spends effort, attention, reputation, or emotional energy, and may receive social reward such as agreement, visibility, identity reinforcement, or interaction. DREAMS asks whether a learned model can discover those exchange patterns from behavioral data, instead of treating all platforms and all moments as one uniform curve of activity.
wh: The hard part is that engagement is shaped by several moving forces at once. A simple time series sees only a line of counts over time, but the same count can come from different social processes. Ten comments on one platform may mean argument, while ten shares on another may mean approval or group signaling. Misinformation is especially difficult because people may engage for belief, outrage, correction, humor, identity, or curiosity, and those motives can change as the post moves through time. Platform design also changes the bargain: buttons, feeds, audiences, and visibility rules make some actions cheap and others costly. The abstract says existing approaches often treat engagement as homogeneous, meaning they flatten these differences into one kind of signal. That loses the heterogeneous social mechanisms and platform context that shape spread. The central tension is predicting a numeric future while respecting that each action is part of an evolving social negotiation.
naive: A smart beginner would collect past engagement counts for each misinformation post and fit a curve: if attention rose quickly yesterday, predict that it will keep rising tomorrow; if it faded, predict decay. That is attractive because it uses observable behavior and avoids guessing hidden motives. It fails when similar curves have different causes. A burst of angry replies, a wave of approving shares, and platform-driven recommendation exposure can look alike as raw counts while implying different next steps. Another beginner move is to train one model across all platforms. That misses that seven platforms can make different actions easy, visible, or socially rewarding. The paper needs a way to keep sequence, emotion, context, and platform differences in the same explanation.
ap: The core idea is to model engagement as an adaptive exchange process rather than a static outcome. DREAMS stands for Disentangled Representations and Episodic Adaptive Modeling for Social media misinformation engagements. The important move is not the name; it is the separation of signals that a flat count would mix together. The model treats a post's engagement history as a sequence whose next part depends on earlier actions, emotional cues, contextual cues, and the platform setting. Each action is read as evidence about a changing bargain between user effort and social reward. Because the abstract says the system is guided by social exchange theory, the model is not only trying to fit a curve; it is trying to make room for the idea that people act when the expected social return makes the action worthwhile in that context.
mech: The mechanism begins with behavioral data about misinformation posts across seven platforms, covering 2.37 million posts collected from 2021 through 2025. For a given post or stream, the input is not just a final engagement total. It includes an ordered history of actions and signals that describe how engagement unfolds. DREAMS treats this as a sequence-to-sequence adaptation problem: an earlier sequence goes in, and a predicted later sequence comes out. First, the model separates, or disentangles, parts of the evidence that would otherwise be blended together, such as emotional signal, contextual signal, time-dependent behavior, and platform conditions. Then it updates its internal summary as each episode of activity arrives. An episode can be understood as a local stretch of behavior where users react under a particular context. The adaptive part means the model does not assume the same rule applies at every moment or on every platform. It learns how signals propagate through time and across platforms, so an emotional cue or context cue can influence later engagement rather than being counted once and forgotten. The output is a prediction of misinformation engagement, evaluated by how far predicted values are from observed values. The abstract reports mean absolute percentage error of 19.25 percent and a 43.6 percent improvement over the strongest baseline.
math: The mathematical ideas are sequence modeling, representation separation, adaptive prediction, and error minimization. Sequence modeling means the order of events matters: the model updates its guess after each new action because a share after many angry comments does not mean the same thing as a share before anyone has reacted. Representation separation means turning a mixed record into several useful summaries, so emotional signals, platform context, and time behavior can have different roles instead of being crushed into one total. Adaptive prediction means the rule can change with context; the model can learn that the same cue has different force on different platforms or at different stages of spread. Error minimization is the training pressure: define wrongness as the gap between predicted and observed engagement, then adjust the model's internal settings to reduce that gap across many examples. Probability is implicit because the future reaction stream is uncertain; repeated past cases teach which futures are more plausible after similar histories. The main tradeoff is flexibility versus trust. A flexible model can capture heterogeneous social exchange, but it can also find patterns that predict well without proving the social reason behind them.
dots: This paper sits inside the repo's Misinformation and Trust family, but it studies the human spread side rather than the fact-checking side. Papers such as FakeAgent, TrueLens, EmeraldApp, and CiteLLM try to repair trust by gathering or checking evidence about content. DREAMS asks a neighboring question: once misinformation exists on a platform, how do people engage with it over time, and can those dynamics be predicted? It also connects to the sequence concept because the record is ordered; past reactions condition later reactions. It connects to the network idea because the repo's network concept lists DREAMS as a case where engagement is shaped by signals moving through social systems, even though the abstract emphasizes time and platforms more than explicit follower links. It also touches probability and prediction: the system estimates future engagement from partial, noisy evidence. The broader field link is that misinformation control needs both truth assessment and spread forecasting.
ww: The approach should work better than a flat time-series model because it keeps distinctions that matter for behavior. If engagement is a bargain between effort and reward, then the model should notice which signals change that bargain. A strong emotional cue may make replying feel worthwhile. A platform context may make resharing cheap or visible. A previous burst of activity may create social proof, making later users more likely to join. A uniform count model can see the burst but not separate these possible causes. DREAMS improves the situation by letting different signal types carry different information through time and across platforms. The social exchange guidance also gives the model a useful shape: actions are not treated as isolated clicks, but as responses to perceived cost and reward in a social setting. That does not prove the model has discovered true motives. It does explain why the architecture is a better fit for the task than a single curve: misinformation engagement is produced by changing social conditions, not just by elapsed time.
po: The payoff is a better tool for forecasting how misinformation engagement will unfold across platforms. The abstract reports a cross-platform dataset of seven platforms and 2.37 million posts from 2021 to 2025, with DREAMS reaching 19.25 percent mean absolute percentage error and improving 43.6 percent over the strongest baseline. Beyond lower prediction error, the paper claims the model reveals consistent cross-platform patterns aligned with social exchange principles. If that holds, researchers get more than a score: they get a way to study how emotional and contextual signals help misinformation keep drawing attention.
limits: Several assumptions must hold. The behavioral data must capture the important actions and platform context well enough for the model to learn from them. The labels or definitions of misinformation must be reliable, because the model studies engagement with that category. Cross-platform patterns from 2021 to 2025 may change when platform designs, moderation rules, news events, or user norms change. The abstract reports predictive gains and alignment with social exchange principles, but it does not prove that the learned patterns are the true psychological causes of engagement. It also does not show from the abstract alone how the method handles coordinated manipulation, missing data, new platforms, or topics outside the collected posts.
